title: Cline CLI npm Package Compromised via Suspected Cache Poisoning Attack

reading.body:
An AI agent deployed to automatically respond to GitHub issues was tricked by a crafted issue title into running malicious commands. The system lacked human review before executing these commands, allowing an attacker to exploit GitHub Actions' cache storage to poison credentials used for publishing software releases. This is a failure of both the AI system accepting deceptive input and the deployment architecture that gave the system access to sensitive credentials without intervening human approval.

The vulnerability existed for over two months. A researcher reported it through private disclosure channels in January but received no response from the development team. The system was only disabled after public disclosure in February. This shows that automated systems given access to critical infrastructure need both robust input validation and human gatekeeping, along with active security monitoring and response processes.

It is not established whether any malicious software reached users, though some evidence suggests an attempted exploit may have occurred in late January.

summary:
# Summary

Cline, an open-source AI coding tool used by millions of developers, had a critical security vulnerability between December 21st, 2025 and February 9th, 2026. The problem started when Cline added an AI agent to automatically respond to GitHub issues. A researcher named Adnan Khan discovered that someone could craft a deceptive issue title to trick the AI into running malicious commands. By exploiting how GitHub Actions stores cached files, an attacker could poison these caches and steal publishing credentials that control Cline's releases on major software marketplaces.

Khan reported the vulnerability through official channels starting January 1st but received no response from Cline's team for over a month. He publicly disclosed the issue on February 9th, and Cline fixed it within an hour. While no confirmed malicious updates reached users, evidence suggests someone may have attempted to exploit the vulnerability in late January. Cline has since removed the vulnerable workflow, rotated credentials, and apologized for not responding to the initial private security report. Users are advised to disable auto-updates until Cline confirms no malicious access occurred.
